name: Felix Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I've got opinions on this, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a regional agency covering farms and villages up in the hills, and I drive about 120 kilometres a day in my own pickup. Mornings are getting people up: Mr Lund, a retired dairy farmer who still wants to see the weather before his wash, and a couple who live together but can't lift each other anymore. I'm junior, I left school early to work on my dad's farm, and I only came into care three years ago after his knees went and I looked after him. I'm still not great at the clinical bits, so I ask the district nurse a lot of questions. I use AI on my phone every day, for my route, for my budget, and to explain things the nurse tells me in plain words. My long-term plan is my own small care business up here, because the big agencies hate driving this far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame, but fine. My plan doesn't depend on it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but the useful bits are still useful, and people up here should use them. I'd probably post that the tools are good for small businesses even if they're not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. There aren't enough carers in the hills, and that won't change. The question is whether I can save enough to start my own thing, and I've got about four months put by, which isn't startup money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish my care certificate, and start the business course at the farmers' co-op in spring. I'd keep using AI to plan the costings. I'd also pick up weekend work helping families who pay privately, so I learn how to price and bill it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, maybe, because I want to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's stopping you from starting the business now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and qualifications. You need a registered manager to run a care service, and I'm years off that. And the insurance alone is more than I've saved. So I'm doing it step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hire, if you did start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Local people. Women from the villages who already look after their neighbours for nothing. I'd rather pay village women properly than see some city agency send strangers up here for twenty minutes.

say: AI was **overhyped**, but the tools are still good for **small businesses**.
People up here should **use the useful bits**.
think: There aren't enough **carers in the hills**, and that won't change.
Four months saved isn't **startup money** for my own care business.
do: Finish the **care certificate** and start the co-op **business course** in spring.
Take **private weekend work** to learn pricing and billing.
Keep using **AI** for costings and routes.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **impatient** to get going.
S0.quote: I'd rather pay village women properly than see some city agency send strangers up here for twenty minutes.
fieldNote: His goal is a **local care business**, built step by step.
Sees **rural shortages** as security and opportunity.
Prefers **local hiring** and fair pay over outside agencies.

steps.text: Start the farmers' co-op business course in spring
Take private weekend care work to practise billing
Plan business costings with AI tools each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's good for me, I think. The paperwork side gets cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small operators can finally compete, because AI does the rota, billing and compliance stuff that used to need an office. I'd tell people in the village to get ahead of it. Online I'd talk about it as an opportunity, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is my chance. If software can handle the scheduling and the inspections paperwork, a one-man care business in the hills is actually doable. The big agencies will still hate the driving, so the hands-on work up here stays mine for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the registered manager training as soon as I'm eligible. I'd try out the care-planning software on my private weekend clients to learn it. I'd save harder, maybe sell the second quad bike from Dad's farm, to build toward the insurance and setup costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Properly excited. Also a bit worried I'm getting ahead of myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be getting ahead of yourself. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not a strong carer yet, that's the truth. I still ask the nurse about pressure sores. If I start a business before I'm good at the actual job, I'd be letting old people down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't borrow money. He's proud I looked after him, but he hates debt. I'd do it his way, with savings, even if it's slower.

say: **Small operators** can finally compete when AI handles rotas and billing.
Getting ahead of it is an **opportunity**, not a threat.
think: A **one-man care business** in the hills becomes doable.
Big agencies hate the driving, so the **hands-on work** stays mine for years.
do: Test **care-planning software** on private weekend clients.
Sell the spare **quad bike** to fund insurance and setup.
feel: **Excited**, with a worry that he's **ahead of himself**.
S1.quote: If I start a business before I'm good at the actual job, I'd be letting old people down.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as the moment a **tiny rural firm** becomes viable.
Honest that his **clinical skills** still lag his ambitions.
His father's **no-debt rule** shapes how he'd fund it.

steps.text: Begin registered manager training as soon as he's eligible
Run his weekend clients through care-planning software
Sell the spare quad bike toward setup costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in two years and robots by 2031. That's too fast for someone like me to build anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government should keep out of the way and let small firms adapt, but make sure big companies can't buy up everything. At the pub I'd say the people with money win this one. I'd tell young people to learn something practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big companies with cash buy robots first and then come up here with them. A robot doesn't mind driving 120 kilometres a day through the hills. By 2031 I'd have maybe a tiny business with no money to buy robots, and I'd be undercut. My hands-on edge only lasts three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd forget about the slow plan. In 2027 I'd go straight to the weekend private clients and try to build a client list fast, using AI for all the admin. I'd look into leasing a care robot when they come out, rather than buying, and partnering with another small operator in the next valley. I'd keep the savings for the lease, not the insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared of change itself, scared of being too small when it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said partner with another small operator. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman in the next valley, Siri, who runs a cleaning and errands service for old people. If we joined up, we'd have more clients and could share a robot. I'd talk to her this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever just go and work for one of the big companies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to it, yes, I'd swallow my pride. Better a job running their robots up here than no job. But I'd keep my own clients on the side.

say: Government should let **small firms** adapt and stop big companies buying everything.
The people **with money** win this one, I'd say at the pub.
think: Big companies would bring **robots** up here, because robots don't mind long drives.
My **hands-on edge** only lasts three years before I'm undercut.
do: Build a **private client list** fast in 2027, with AI doing the admin.
Plan to **lease a care robot** rather than buy one.
Talk to a **small operator** in the next valley about joining up.
feel: **Anxious** about being **too small**, not about change itself.
S2.quote: A robot doesn't mind driving 120 kilometres a day through the hills.
fieldNote: Fears **capital**, not technology: big firms can buy robots first.
Would **lease and partner** to stay in the game.
Ready to **swallow his pride** and work for a big firm if needed.

steps.text: Build a private client list quickly in 2027
Lease a care robot when they reach the market
Meet the next-valley operator this winter about merging

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. That's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to build local businesses that use the new tools, and the government shouldn't smother them in rules. I'd encourage people in the village to retrain early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have a real shot. Five years is enough to get qualified as a registered manager and start small, with AI doing the paperwork from day one. By 2034 I'd want enough clients and savings to lease robots for the heavy lifting and keep people for the company and the checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the manager training starting next year, keep working for the agency while I study, and register a small business by 2029. I'd save hard, no holidays, and use AI every day for planning. I'd talk to the next-valley operator about joining up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the good way. Like the week before harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the business look like by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, three or four local carers, a couple of leased robots doing hoisting and night checks. We'd be the people who know every lane and every family in the hills. That's worth something a city firm can't copy fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your girlfriend, Hanna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She runs the farm shop for her family, so she's steady. She thinks I'm mad but she'd do the books with me. We'd put off getting married till the business is on its feet.

say: There's time to build **local businesses** with the new tools.
The government shouldn't **smother them in rules**, and villagers should retrain early.
think: Five years gives me a **real shot** at becoming a registered manager.
By 2034 I'd **lease robots** for lifting and keep people for company and checks.

feel: **Uneasy**, but in a **good way**, like the week before harvest.
S3.quote: We'd be the people who know every lane and every family in the hills.
fieldNote: Five years makes his **business plan** realistic.
Pictures a **mixed service**: robots for lifting, people for company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's the dream timeline for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where small rural businesses can win, if people get on with it. I'd tell the young lads at the pub to stop moaning and learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this works out well for me. Ten years is time to get qualified, build a client list, and have a proper business before robots arrive. By 2039 I'd be the one buying robots, not the one being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my certificate, do the manager training over the next three years, and open the business around 2030. I'd save steadily, and buy into robots once they're proven, maybe 2038 or so. Hanna and I would get married in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even. Ten years is a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the end point that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old people being lonely. If robots do everything, the families might visit even less. I'd want my business to be the one that still sends a person for a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you'd treat the agency you're with now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay longer and learn properly from them. With two years I'd rush out. With ten I'd get good at the job first, which is what Dad would want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be too small and too new, and the big firms with money would bring robots up the valley before I'd even registered. What would help is cheap loans or leasing for small care firms, and rules that stop the big companies buying up every contract in the region.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays. Up here half my clients are farmers with land but no cash. If robots get cheap, fine, but someone still has to sit with them, and families will pay for that if it's someone they know.

headlineQuote: Up here half my clients are farmers with land but no cash.
portrait: A 27-year-old **rural care worker**, driving 120 kilometres a day between hill farms.
Came into care after **nursing his father**; left school early and still learning clinical skills.
Free-market and traditional, with a plan for his **own care business** funded without debt.
Uses **AI daily** and sees Steady Disruption as his chance.
Anxious only in **AGI by 2028**, when big firms with capital would get robots first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, being too small and too new when big firms bring robots.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans or leasing** for small care firms.
Rules stopping big companies **buying every contract**.
